questions.title: Technical specification
questions.text: Which statement best defines a **technical specification** of a new system?

options.content: A list of the hardware and software needed to run the new system, with the figures and a reason for each choice
A user guide that explains how to use the new system
The program code of the new system
A report that evaluates the old system

scheme.mark_scheme: A
scheme.explanation: A technical specification is a design document: it lists the hardware and software (with figures such as GB and GHz) and justifies each choice.

questions.title: Minimum RAM
questions.text: A new system needs an operating system (minimum 4 GB RAM), a DBMS (2 GB) and the library application (1 GB), all running at the same time. Which is the **smallest suitable** amount of RAM for the specification?

scheme.mark_scheme: C
scheme.explanation: All three programs run at the same time, so their RAM is added: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 GB; the smallest standard size that fits is 8 GB.

questions.title: Minimum processor speed
questions.text: The OS needs a 1 GHz processor, the DBMS 2.4 GHz and the booking app 1.8 GHz. What is the **minimum processor speed** for the specification?

scheme.mark_scheme: C
scheme.explanation: Processor speeds are not added: the processor must satisfy the most demanding program, so take the highest — 2.4 GHz.

questions.title: Minimum storage
questions.text: A new system needs: operating system 64 GB, DBMS 10 GB, application 6 GB. The database is 20 GB now and grows by 5 GB per year. Calculate the minimum storage (in GB) needed for the system to last **4 years**. Give the number only.

scheme.mark_scheme: Software 64 + 10 + 6 = 80 GB; data 20 + 4 × 5 = 40 GB; total **120 GB**.
scheme.explanation: Storage is added: all the software + the data now + the growth of the data over the life of the system.

questions.title: How the minimum is found
questions.text:
Complete the rules for determining the minimum hardware requirements.

For the processor, take the [[1]] requirement of all the software. For RAM, [[2]] the requirements of all programs that run at the same time. For storage, add the size of all the software, the data and its expected [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) highest / largest / biggest / maximum / fastest (2) add / sum / total / add up (3) growth / increase
scheme.explanation: Speeds are never added; memory and storage are.

questions.title: RAM and storage
questions.text: RAM stores the software and data of a system **permanently**, even when the computer is switched off.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: RAM is main memory: it is volatile and holds only the programs and data in use. Permanent storage is the SSD / HDD.

questions.title: Components and units
questions.text: Match each hardware component to what is specified for it.

right.text: Capacity of main memory in GB
Wired or Wi-Fi and bandwidth in Mbps
Type (SSD / HDD) and capacity in GB or TB
Clock speed in GHz and number of cores

scheme.mark_scheme: Processor – Clock speed in GHz and number of cores; RAM – Capacity of main memory in GB; Storage – Type (SSD / HDD) and capacity in GB or TB; Display – Screen size and resolution, e.g. 1920 × 1080; Network card – Wired or Wi-Fi and bandwidth in Mbps. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Input or output
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the device is an input or an output device of the system.

prefill: Barcode scanner at a library desk
Thermal receipt printer at a checkout
ID-card reader at a clinic reception
Touchscreen used to choose a product
Speaker that announces the next patient

scheme.mark_scheme: Barcode scanner at a library desk – Input (1); Thermal receipt printer at a checkout – Output (1); ID-card reader at a clinic reception – Input (1); Customer display showing the price – Output (1); Touchscreen used to choose a product – Input (1); Speaker that announces the next patient – Output (1)

questions.title: Devices for a checkout
questions.text: A supermarket is introducing a new checkout system. Products are scanned, customers pay by card and get a paper receipt. Select the **three** devices this system needs.

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Each device comes from an input or output of the system: scanning → barcode scanner, paying by card → card terminal, receipt → thermal printer.

questions.title: Why an SSD
questions.text: Why might an **SSD** be chosen instead of an HDD for the computer that runs a clinic's database?

options.content: It is always cheaper per GB than an HDD
It has faster access, so patient records open quickly
It can store more data than any HDD
It does not need an operating system

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: An SSD has faster access times and no moving parts; an HDD is cheaper per GB and is good for large backups.

questions.title: Above the minimum
questions.text: Select **three** reasons why a designer specifies hardware **above** the minimum requirements.

options.content: The amount of data grows every year
New versions of the software usually need more resources
The most expensive hardware is always the best choice
Users often run several programs at the same time
The minimum requirements are always wrong
Above the minimum no backup is needed

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Growth of data, updates and several programs at once all need extra resources — but the specification must still be justified, not simply the most expensive.

questions.title: System or application software
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of software.

scheme.mark_scheme: Windows 11 – System software (1); MySQL database management system – Application software (1); Antivirus program – System software (1); Library loans program – Application software (1); Linux – System software (1); Spreadsheet – Application software (1)
scheme.explanation: Operating systems and utilities (antivirus, backup) run the computer; application software does a task for the user.

questions.title: Software criteria
questions.text: A designer asks: *"Will this software run on the chosen hardware and operating system, and can it import our existing data?"* Which criterion is this?

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Compatibility: the software must run on the chosen hardware and OS and work with the existing data.

questions.title: Justifications and criteria
questions.text: Match each justification to the criterion it uses.

left.text: It is free, so the school pays no licence fees for 30 computers
It runs on the school's Linux server
The interface is in Kazakh and the nurses learn it quickly
Patient records are encrypted and each user has access rights
It can handle the extra branches the shop plans to open
The supplier runs a help desk and releases regular updates

scheme.mark_scheme: It is free, so the school pays no licence fees for 30 computers – Cost; It runs on the school's Linux server – Compatibility; The interface is in Kazakh and the nurses learn it quickly – Ease of use; Patient records are encrypted and each user has access rights – Security; It can handle the extra branches the shop plans to open – Scalability; The supplier runs a help desk and releases regular updates – Support. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Price only
questions.text: When choosing software for a new system, it is enough to choose the cheapest product that is available.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Software must also meet the requirements and be compatible, easy to use, supported, secure and able to grow.

questions.title: Off-the-shelf software
questions.text: Select **two** advantages of **off-the-shelf** software compared with bespoke software.

options.content: It does exactly what one organisation needs
It is usually cheaper because many customers share the cost
Only the organisation can use it
It is written by the organisation's own programmers

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Bespoke software fits the needs exactly but is expensive and takes time to develop; off-the-shelf is cheaper, available now and already tested by many users.

questions.title: Open source or proprietary
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement describes open-source or proprietary software.

prefill: The source code can be studied and changed
Users pay a licence fee or subscription
Only the company that owns it can change it
Usually free, with support from a community

scheme.mark_scheme: The source code can be studied and changed – Open source (1); Users pay a licence fee or subscription – Proprietary (1); Only the company that owns it can change it – Proprietary (1); Usually free, with support from a community – Open source (1); Example: Microsoft Access – Proprietary (1); Example: LibreOffice – Open source (1)

questions.title: Open source and freeware
questions.text: A program is free to download, but its source code cannot be seen or changed. What type of software is it?

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Freeware is free but closed source. Open-source software makes the source code available.

questions.title: Best justification
questions.text: A clinic with five receptionists chooses a booking package. Which is the **best justification**?

options.content: It is a good and popular program
Five receptionists can book at the same time without double-booking a dentist, which the clinic needs at busy times
It was the first program the manager found

scheme.mark_scheme: C
scheme.explanation: A justification links a feature of the software (multi-user access) to a need of this scenario (five receptionists, busy times).

questions.title: Complete the specification
questions.text:
A shop's new stock system runs these programs **at the same time**. The stock data needs 30 GB.

| Software | Processor | RAM | Storage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating system | 1.5 GHz | 4 GB | 40 GB |
| DBMS | 2.2 GHz | 4 GB | 8 GB |
| Stock application | 2 GHz | 2 GB | 2 GB |

Complete the minimum specification. Give numbers only.

scheme.mark_scheme: Processor 2.2 GHz — the highest (1); RAM 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 GB (1); storage 40 + 8 + 2 + 30 = 80 GB (1)
scheme.explanation: Take the highest processor speed; add the RAM of programs that run together; add all software and the data for storage.

questions.title: Hardware for a school library
questions.text:
**Aqbota School** is introducing a new library system. The librarian's computer will run these programs **at the same time**:

| Software | Processor | RAM | Storage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating system | 1 GHz | 4 GB | 64 GB |
| DBMS | 2.4 GHz | 2 GB | 10 GB |
| Library application | 1.8 GHz | 2 GB | 6 GB |

The database of books and loans will need **20 GB**.

scheme.mark_scheme: - the lowest specification of hardware on which the software / system will still run (correctly) (1)
scheme.model_answer: The lowest specification of hardware (processor, RAM, storage) on which the system's software will still run correctly.

parts.title: Calculate the minimum
parts.text: Complete the table with the minimum specification for the librarian's computer. Give numbers only.

scheme.mark_scheme: Processor 2.4 GHz (1); RAM 4 + 2 + 2 = 8 GB (1); storage 64 + 10 + 6 + 20 = 100 GB (1)
scheme.model_answer: Processor 2.4 GHz; RAM 8 GB; storage 100 GB.

parts.title: Processor speed
parts.text: Explain why the minimum processor speed is **not** found by adding the three processor speeds.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- clock speed is a property of one processor / the processor runs all the programs (1)
- it must only be fast enough for the most demanding program, so the highest value is taken (1)
scheme.model_answer: The speed is a property of the one processor that runs all the programs; it only has to meet the most demanding program, so the highest value (2.4 GHz) is used, not the sum.

parts.title: Above the minimum
parts.text: The IT teacher specifies a computer **above** the minimum you calculated. Explain **two** reasons for this decision.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two reasons, each identified (1) and explained in context (1):
- the database grows as books / loans are added (1) — storage / RAM would run out in a few years (1)
- updates of the OS / software need more resources (1) — the computer would become too slow / unable to install updates (1)
- several programs open at once, e.g. browser + library app (1) — at the bare minimum the system is slow and students wait (1)
- more users / terminals added later (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every year new books and loans are added, so the 20 GB database grows and 100 GB would soon be full. Also new versions of Windows and the DBMS usually need more RAM, so at exactly 8 GB the computer would become slow and students would wait at the desk.

questions.title: Devices for a supermarket checkout
questions.text: **Arzan Market**, a supermarket in Pavlodar, is replacing its tills. At each new checkout the cashier scans the products, the customer pays by bank card and receives a paper receipt. All checkouts send sales to a **server** in the office, which stores the stock database.

parts.title: Input devices
parts.text: Identify **two input devices** needed at each checkout. Give a reason for each.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two devices (1 each) with a reason linked to the scenario (1 each):
- barcode scanner (1) — reads product codes quickly / without typing errors (1)
- card payment terminal / card reader (1) — customers pay by bank card (1)
- touchscreen / keyboard (1) — cashier enters items without barcodes, e.g. fruit / quantities (1)
- weighing scales (1) — loose products priced by weight (1)
scheme.model_answer: A barcode scanner, so each product's code is read quickly and without typing mistakes. A card payment terminal, because customers pay by bank card.

parts.title: Output device
parts.text: Identify **one output device** needed at each checkout and give a reason.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- thermal / receipt printer (1) — every customer receives a paper receipt (1)
- accept customer display — shows the price / total to the customer (1)
scheme.model_answer: A thermal receipt printer, because every customer must get a paper receipt.

parts.title: SSD for the server
parts.text: Explain why an **SSD** is suitable for storing the stock database on the server.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- faster access / read-write than an HDD (1)
- so sales from all checkouts are saved / stock is updated quickly / customers do not wait (1)
- accept: no moving parts, more reliable, so data is less likely to be lost (1)
scheme.model_answer: An SSD has much faster access than an HDD, so the sales from all the checkouts are recorded and the stock levels updated immediately and customers do not wait.

parts.title: Network
parts.text: Explain why each checkout computer needs a **network card**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the checkouts must send sales / read prices from the server / shared database (1)
- so stock levels are updated in one place / all tills use the same prices (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each checkout must be connected to the server so it can read the current prices and send every sale to the stock database, keeping the stock levels up to date for all tills.

questions.title: Software for a dental clinic
questions.text: **Ak Tis**, a dental clinic in Shymkent, has 4 receptionists who book about 120 appointments a day. Patient records are confidential. The receptionists have little IT experience, and the clinic wants the new system working **next month**.

parts.title: Types of software
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the software is system software or application software.

scheme.mark_scheme: Windows 11 – System software (1); Appointment booking package – Application software (1); Automatic backup utility – System software (1)
scheme.model_answer: Windows 11 – System software; Appointment booking package – Application software; Automatic backup utility – System software.

parts.title: Off-the-shelf
parts.text: The manager chooses an **off-the-shelf** booking package instead of **bespoke** software. Justify this choice.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 points, each linked to the clinic:
- available immediately (1) — the clinic wants the system next month; bespoke would take months to write (1)
- cheaper (1) — the development cost is shared by many clinics (1)
- already tested by many users / fewer bugs (1); tutorials / support / updates available for receptionists with little IT experience (1)
- already has the features a clinic needs, e.g. appointments, reminders (1)
Max 2 marks if no link to the scenario.
scheme.model_answer: An off-the-shelf package can be installed now, which matters because the clinic wants it next month — bespoke software would take months to develop. It is also cheaper, because many clinics share its cost, and it has already been tested by many users, with tutorials that help receptionists who have little IT experience.

parts.title: More than price
parts.text: Explain why the clinic should **not** choose the booking software on price alone. Refer to **two** other criteria.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the cheapest software may not meet the requirements / functionality (1)
- security: patient records are confidential, so it needs user accounts / access rights / encryption (1)
- ease of use: receptionists have little IT experience, so it must be easy to learn / in their language (1)
- multi-user: 4 receptionists book at the same time (1); compatibility with existing PCs (1); support (1)
Max 3.
scheme.model_answer: The cheapest program might not do what the clinic needs. It must be secure, because patient records are confidential and need passwords and access rights, and it must be easy to use, because the receptionists have little IT experience.

questions.title: Office software for a college
questions.text: **Turan College** is buying office software for **200** computers in its classrooms. The budget is small. The college IT technician would like to adapt the software for the college's own templates. Two options are considered: a **proprietary** office suite with a yearly subscription, and an **open-source** office suite.

parts.title: Differences
parts.text: State **two** differences between open-source and proprietary software.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- open source: source code available and can be changed; proprietary: code closed (1)
- open source usually free; proprietary needs a licence fee / subscription (1)
- open source: community support; proprietary: official support from the company (1)
scheme.model_answer: Open-source software has source code that anyone can see and change, while proprietary code is closed. Open-source software is usually free, while proprietary software needs a licence fee or subscription.

parts.title: Recommend
parts.text: Recommend which office suite the college should choose. Justify your recommendation using **three** criteria.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Recommendation (either accepted if justified). Three criteria, each identified (1) and linked to the college (1):
- cost (1) — no subscription for 200 computers on a small budget (1)
- adaptability / source code (1) — the technician can change it for the college's templates (1)
- compatibility (1) — opens / saves files in the formats used by teachers / runs on the college's OS (1)
- support (1) — community forums / tutorials, or official support if proprietary chosen (1)
- ease of use (1) — familiar interface, little training for teachers and students (1)
No recommendation: max 5.
scheme.model_answer: The open-source suite. Cost: it is free, so the college pays no subscription for 200 computers, which suits the small budget. Adaptability: its source code is available, so the technician can change it to add the college's own templates. Compatibility: it can open and save Microsoft Office formats, so teachers can still use files they receive from others.

parts.title: Utility software
parts.text: Identify **one** utility program that should be included in the technical specification and give a reason.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- antivirus (1) — protects 200 networked computers / files from malware (1)
- backup utility (1) — students' / teachers' files can be restored if lost (1)
- accept disk clean-up / compression / firewall with a reason (1)
scheme.model_answer: Antivirus software, because 200 classroom computers are used by many students with USB drives and the Internet, so malware could spread across the network.

summary: Writing a technical specification for a new system — determining the minimum hardware requirements (processor, RAM, storage, display, network, input and output devices) from the software and the data, and justifying the choice of system and application software with criteria linked to the scenario.

blocks.content: A document, written at the **design stage**, that lists the **hardware and software needed to implement and run a new system**, with the exact figures (e.g. RAM in GB, storage in GB, processor speed) and a **reason for every choice**.

The **lowest specification of each hardware component** (processor, RAM, storage, display, network, peripherals) with which the new system — its operating system, application software and data — **will still run correctly**. Below the minimum the software will not install, or will be too slow to use.

A higher specification, suggested by the software developer, with which the software runs **comfortably** — quickly, with several programs open and with room for growth. A good technical specification is **at least the minimum** and usually close to the **recommended** figures.

blocks.text: Why a technical specification is written

blocks.content: A new system is not only a program. It is a **combination of hardware, system software, application software and data** that must work together from the first day. During analysis the developers find out *what* the system must do: how many users there are, what is input, what is output and how much data is kept. At the **design stage** these requirements are turned into a technical specification, which answers the question *"what exactly must be bought and installed so that the system works?"*.

The specification is used by several people. The **client** (for example the school director) uses it to approve the budget, because every item has a price. The **supplier** uses it to order the right computers and devices. The **technician** uses it to install and configure the equipment, and the **developer** uses it to make sure the software is tested on the same kind of hardware that the users will have. Because so many people rely on it, the specification must contain **exact figures with units** (8 GB, 2.5 GHz, 256 GB SSD, 1920 × 1080) and not vague words such as "fast" or "big".

Every line also needs a **reason**. A reason shows that the figure was **calculated from the requirements** and was not simply copied from an advertisement. If the client asks "why do we need 16 GB of RAM and not 8 GB?", the reason in the specification answers that question. This is also why exam questions on this topic almost always say *"justify"* or *"give a reason for each"*: a device or a figure without a reason earns at most half of the marks.

The specification deliberately describes the **minimum** that is needed. If the hardware is below the minimum, the software may refuse to install, crash, or be so slow that users stop using it. If it is far above the minimum, the organisation wastes money that could be spent on training or support. A good specification is therefore **just above the minimum**, with a sensible margin for growth.

blocks.caption: How the minimum hardware requirements are determined

blocks.title: Hardware components in a technical specification
rows: The **highest** minimum of all the software; more for video, graphics, many users
**Add** the RAM of the OS and of every program that runs **at the same time**
Type (SSD / HDD) and capacity in GB / TB
**Add** the size of all software + the data now + the **growth** of the data + backups
Design, video and CAD need a high resolution and a graphics card
Needed if data is **shared** or the system is **online**; more bandwidth for many users
Keyboard, mouse, barcode scanner, touchscreen, camera, card reader, microphone
Systems that must never lose data or stop

blocks.title: Worked example — a school library system
blocks.content:
The library will run **Windows** (min. 4 GB RAM, 1 GHz, 64 GB), a **DBMS** (min. 2 GB RAM, 2 GHz, 4 GB) and the **library application** (min. 1 GB RAM, 1.5 GHz, 1 GB) **at the same time**. The database is 6 GB now and grows by about **2 GB per year**; the system should last **5 years**.

- **Processor:** the highest minimum is **2 GHz** (the DBMS) → specify at least a **2 GHz** processor (the speeds are **not** added).
- **RAM:** all three run together → 4 + 2 + 1 = **7 GB** → the next standard size is **8 GB**.
- **Storage:** software 64 + 4 + 1 = 69 GB; data 6 + 5 × 2 = 16 GB → 85 GB → specify **128 GB** (or 256 GB to allow backups).
- **Input:** a **barcode scanner** — books and student cards have barcodes, so loans are recorded quickly and without typing errors.
- **Output:** a **printer** for loan slips and overdue letters.
- **Network:** a **network card** — the database is shared with the librarian's and teachers' computers.

items.title: Processor
items.content:
- Clock speed in **GHz** — how many instructions per second.
- More **cores** → several tasks at once (many users on a server).
- Take the **highest** requirement, never the sum.

items.title: RAM
items.content:
- Holds the OS, the programs and the data **currently in use**.
- Too little RAM → the computer uses **virtual memory** and becomes slow.
- **Add** the needs of programs that run together; round up to 4 / 8 / 16 GB.

items.title: Storage
items.content:
- Stores software and data **permanently**.
- **SSD**: faster access, no moving parts, quieter — good for databases.
- **HDD**: cheaper per GB — good for large backups and archives.

items.title: Peripherals
items.content:
- Chosen from the system's **inputs and outputs**.
- Each device needs a **reason**: "a barcode scanner, because …".

blocks.text: How each component affects the system

blocks.content: **The processor** carries out the instructions of every program. Its **clock speed**, measured in gigahertz (GHz), tells us how many cycles it performs per second, and the number of **cores** tells us how many instructions it can work on at the same time. A program's minimum processor requirement means "the program needs a processor at least this fast to respond in an acceptable time". Because one processor runs all the programs by sharing its time between them, the requirements are **not added**: a 2.5 GHz processor is fast enough for a program that needs 2 GHz *and* for one that needs 1.5 GHz. We therefore take the **highest** minimum. More cores are needed when the work can be split up — a **server** that answers many users at once, video editing, or 3D graphics.

**RAM** is the main memory. It holds the operating system, every program that is **open** and the data those programs are working on **right now**. Unlike the processor, RAM is **divided** between the programs: if Windows uses 4 GB and the DBMS uses 2 GB, those 6 GB cannot be used by anything else. This is why the RAM needs of programs that run **at the same time** are **added**. When RAM runs out, the operating system moves parts of programs to the disk (**virtual memory**); the disk is thousands of times slower than RAM, so the whole computer becomes very slow. RAM is sold in standard sizes (4, 8, 16, 32 GB), so the total is always **rounded up**.

**Storage** (secondary storage) keeps the software and the data **permanently**, even when the power is off. Everything that is installed takes space, so the sizes of the OS and all the programs are added. The **data** must be added too, and data **grows**: a shop adds new sales every day, a clinic adds new patients and scans. The specification is written for the **whole life** of the system (often 3–5 years), so the growth per year is multiplied by the number of years. Space for **backups** and updates is also needed. The **type** of storage matters: an **SSD** has no moving parts and much faster access, so a database answers queries quickly; an **HDD** is cheaper per gigabyte and suits large archives.

**Peripherals** — the input and output devices — come from the **inputs and outputs** of the system found during analysis. If the system reads barcodes, it needs a barcode scanner; if it prints receipts, it needs a receipt printer; if customers pay by card, it needs a card terminal. Each device is chosen because it makes a task **faster, more accurate or possible at all**. Finally the **network**: if the data is shared by several computers, or the system works online, each computer needs a network card and the connection needs enough **bandwidth** (Mbps) for all users at once.

A hardware device connected to the computer to **input** data (keyboard, scanner, camera, card reader) or **output** information (monitor, printer, speakers). In a technical specification each peripheral is chosen from the system's inputs and outputs and given a reason.

blocks.title: Too little or too much hardware
rows: Programs respond slowly; users wait at every screen
Money wasted; the extra speed is never used
Virtual memory is used; the computer freezes when several programs are open
Unused memory; higher price per computer
The disk fills up; no new records or backups can be saved
Paying for space the data will never need
The budget is spent on hardware instead of training or support

blocks.content:
- **Adding processor speeds** (2 + 1.5 + 1 GHz = 4.5 GHz) — speed is not added; take the highest.
- Forgetting the **operating system** when adding RAM or storage.
- Forgetting the **data** and its **growth** — the disk fills up after a year.
- Writing "a fast computer" or "a lot of memory" — the specification needs **figures** (GB, GHz).
- Listing a device without saying **why** this system needs it.
Software that **runs and manages the computer** itself: the **operating system** (Windows, Linux, macOS) and **utility programs** (antivirus, backup, compression, disk tools).
Software that does a **task for the user**: a DBMS (MySQL, Microsoft Access), a spreadsheet, a word processor, a web browser, or a specialised program (library, clinic, accounting).

Give a **reason**, linked to the **needs of the scenario**, why this software is chosen: *software* → *criterion* → *because the system needs …*. A list of features without a link to the scenario is **not** a justification.

Software is chosen **before** the hardware, because the hardware requirements come from the software. The order is usually: first the **application software** that does the user's task (the booking program, the library system, the DBMS), then an **operating system** that this application runs on, then the **utilities** that keep the system safe (antivirus, backup, drivers for the devices). The choice of operating system is often decided by the application: if the clinic's booking package runs only on Windows, the clinic needs Windows, whatever the IT teacher prefers.

For each type of software there are several options, and the developer must **compare them using criteria**. The most important criterion is **functionality**: software that is cheap but cannot do a required task is useless. After that the options are compared on **compatibility** (with the hardware, the OS, other programs and the existing data), **cost**, **ease of use** for these particular users, **support**, **security**, **scalability** and **multi-user access**. No software is best on every criterion. Off-the-shelf software is cheap and available at once but may not fit exactly; bespoke software fits exactly but is expensive and slow to produce. Open-source software has no licence fee but may have less official support. The developer chooses the option whose strengths match the **most important needs of this scenario** — that is what "justify" means.

Cost is more than the purchase price. A licence may be paid **per computer** or **per user**, or as a yearly **subscription**; there may be costs for upgrades, training and support. This total over the life of the system is called the **total cost of ownership**. Free software is not always cheaper in total if staff need a lot of training to use it.

The legal permission to use a piece of software, stating **how many computers or users** may use it, for **how long** and whether the software may be **copied or changed**. The number of licences needed is part of the technical specification.

blocks.title: Off-the-shelf and bespoke software
rows: Bought or downloaded, the **same for many customers**
**Cheaper** — the cost is shared by many users
**Expensive** — programmers are paid to write it
Already tested by many users; forums, tutorials, updates
Bugs may be found later; support only from the developer
A booking system written for one hotel

blocks.title: Proprietary and open-source software
rows: **Closed** — users cannot see or change it
Official support from the company, guaranteed updates
Community forums; paid support from some firms
Only the company can change it
The organisation can **adapt** it to its needs

blocks.title: Criteria for choosing software
rows: Does it do **everything** in the requirements?
"…because it can print overdue letters, which the librarian needs"
Does it run on the chosen **hardware and OS**? Can it **import** the existing data?
"…because it runs on the school's Linux server and imports the old CSV files"
Price of licences for all users, subscription, upgrades, training
"…because it is free, and the school's budget is small"
Can **these users** learn it quickly? Is it in their **language**?
"…because the nurses have little IT experience and the interface is in Kazakh and Russian"
Manuals, tutorials, help desk, regular updates
"…because the supplier offers a help desk during clinic hours"
User accounts, access rights, encryption, backup
"…because patient records are confidential and it encrypts the data"
Can it cope with **more users and data** later?
"…because the shop plans to open two more branches"
Can several people use it **at the same time**?
"…because five receptionists book appointments at once"

blocks.caption: Software for a new system: system software and application software

blocks.title: How to justify a choice of software
items: **Name** the software and its **type** (e.g. "MySQL — an open-source DBMS").
Pick a **criterion** (functionality, compatibility, cost, ease of use, support, security, scalability).
Say **what the software provides** for that criterion.
**Link** it to a **need of the scenario** with "because" / "so that".
Repeat for each mark: one criterion + link = usually **2 marks**.

blocks.title: Worked justification — a dental clinic
blocks.content:
**Scenario:** a clinic in Shymkent with 4 receptionists books 120 appointments a day, keeps confidential patient records and has a small budget. The receptionists have little IT experience.

- **Operating system: Windows 11** — compatible with the clinic's existing PCs and the booking program (1), and the receptionists already know it, so little training is needed (1).
- **Booking software: an off-the-shelf clinic package** (rather than bespoke) — it is available immediately and cheaper because the cost is shared by many clinics (1); it already has appointment booking and SMS reminders, which the clinic needs (1).
- **Security:** it has user accounts with access rights and encrypts patient records, because medical data is confidential (1).
- **Multi-user:** four receptionists can book at the same time without double-booking a dentist (1).

"**It is cheap**" earns little. "**It is free and open source, so the school does not pay licence fees for 30 computers**" earns the mark — the **feature** plus the **reason it matters in this scenario**.

- Naming software with **no reason** ("Use Microsoft Access.").
- Reasons that fit **any** system ("it is good", "it is popular") — link to **this** scenario.
- Choosing only by **price** — the software must first meet the **requirements**.
- Forgetting the **operating system** and **utilities** (antivirus, backup) — they are part of the specification.
- Mixing up **open source** (source code available) with **freeware** (free, but the code is closed).

blocks.text: Hardware and software depend on each other

blocks.content: The two halves of the specification cannot be written separately. The software decides the minimum hardware; but the hardware the organisation **already owns** can also limit the software. If a school has thirty computers with 4 GB of RAM, choosing a program that needs 8 GB means buying thirty new computers or extra memory. In that case a lighter program, or a web-based system that runs on a server, may be the better justified choice. A complete specification therefore shows that **every component is compatible** with every other: the OS supports the devices (there are drivers), the application runs on that OS, and the hardware meets the combined requirements.

The final document is usually a **table** with three columns — component, minimum specification, reason — because a table is easy for the client to read and for the supplier to order from. Software appears in the same table as the hardware, each with its justification. Writing the reason in the same row as the figure makes it clear that every number was **calculated from the requirements**.

blocks.title: How to write a technical specification for a new system
items: Read the **requirements** of the system: tasks, number of users, inputs, outputs, amount of data.
Choose the **software**: operating system, application software (DBMS, specialised program), utilities — and **justify** each choice.
Work out the **processor** (highest), **RAM** (sum of what runs together), **storage** (software + data + growth).
Add the **input and output devices** and the **network** needed by the system.
Add a **margin** for growth and future updates; round up to standard sizes.
Present the specification as a **table**: component — specification — reason.

blocks.title: Technical specification — reception computer at the dental clinic
blocks.content:
| Component | Minimum specification | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Processor | 4 cores, 2.4 GHz | Highest requirement of the booking software; runs the browser and the booking program together |
| RAM | 8 GB | Windows 4 GB + booking software 2 GB + browser 1 GB = 7 GB, rounded up |
| Storage | 256 GB SSD | Software 80 GB + local data and growth; an SSD opens patient records quickly |
| Display | 24″, 1920 × 1080 | The appointment calendar shows all dentists for a whole day |
| Input | Keyboard, mouse, ID-card reader | The card reader enters patient details from ID cards without typing errors |
| Output | Laser printer | Prints invoices and appointment cards |
| Network | Gigabit Ethernet, Internet 50 Mbps | Shared database on the clinic server; SMS reminders sent online |
| Operating system | Windows 11 | Required by the booking software; staff already know it |
| Utilities | Antivirus, automatic daily backup | Protect confidential records from malware and loss |

blocks.title: Why specify above the minimum?
rows: The database gets bigger every year; storage and RAM must cope
New staff or branches add load on the server and network
New versions of the OS and software usually need more resources
Users open a browser, e-mail and the system together
At the bare minimum the system is slow; users waste time
Too far above the minimum wastes money — the specification should be **justified**, not the most expensive

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term minimum hardware requirements. [1]**
The lowest specification of hardware (processor, RAM, storage…) on which the system's software will **still run** correctly (1).

**Q: A system runs an OS (4 GB RAM), a DBMS (2 GB) and an app (2 GB) at the same time. State the minimum RAM and show how you found it. [2]**
4 + 2 + 2 = 8 GB (1) — the programs run together, so their RAM needs are **added** (1).

**Q: A supermarket's new checkout system scans products and prints receipts. Identify two devices it needs and give a reason for each. [4]**
**Barcode scanner** (1) — reads the product codes quickly and without typing errors (1). **Thermal / receipt printer** (1) — prints a receipt for every customer (1). *(Also: card payment terminal, touchscreen, customer display.)*

**Q: Explain why an SSD may be chosen for the computer that runs the clinic's database. [2]**
An SSD has **faster access** than an HDD (1), so patient records open quickly while the patient waits / many queries are answered quickly (1). *(Also: no moving parts — more reliable.)*

**Q: A school chooses open-source software for 30 classroom computers. Justify this choice using two criteria. [4]**
**Cost:** it is free (1), so the school pays no licence fee for 30 computers on a small budget (1). **Compatibility / adaptability:** it runs on the school's Linux computers / the source code can be changed (1), so the IT teacher can adapt it to the school's needs (1).

**Q: State one advantage and one disadvantage of bespoke software for a hotel's booking system. [2]**
Advantage: it does **exactly** what the hotel needs (1). Disadvantage: **expensive** / takes a long time to write / may contain bugs (1).

- Adding processor speeds instead of taking the highest.
- Specifications without **units** (write 8 **GB**, 2.5 **GHz**, 256 **GB SSD**).
- A device or program named with no **reason linked to the scenario**.
- Confusing **RAM** (main memory, temporary) with **storage** (SSD / HDD, permanent).
- Justifying software only by price.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: Define a technical specification, minimum and recommended requirements.
List eight hardware components a specification may include, with a unit for each.
How is the minimum CPU found? The minimum RAM? The minimum storage?
Calculate the RAM and storage for an OS (4 GB, 40 GB), a DBMS (2 GB, 5 GB) and data of 20 GB growing 5 GB a year for 4 years.
Give two input and two output devices for a library, a supermarket and a clinic, with reasons.
Compare off-the-shelf and bespoke software; proprietary and open-source software.
Name eight criteria for choosing software and write one justification linked to a scenario for each.

topic_exam.instructions: Answer **all** questions. Show your working in calculations and link your answers to each scenario. The number of marks is given in brackets [ ] at the end of each part. Total: 40 marks. Time: 50 minutes.
